summary.text: 牛 is a picture of an ox’s head and horns, used for the animal—ox or cattle—and also as a character radical.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph depicts an ox’s head and horns. Early form classes are described as frontal views; some bronze forms are said to include ears, eyes, and nose.

history.text: The transmitted Shuowen description mentions horns, head, and a tail or raised-back feature. It glosses 牛 as a large sacrificial animal. Duan Yucai later offers a different interpretation based on the animal’s work and patterns; these are lexicographic explanations of the graph, not separate evidence for its origin.

Oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and small-seal forms are listed. The small-seal form shown here is a modern rendering of a later form; neither it nor the listed form classes establishes a dated sequence or the earliest surviving specimen.
Use for cattle and personal-name use are both reported in bronze inscriptions, though the cited examples do not establish when either use began.

uncertainties.text: The head-and-horns pictographic analysis is supported, but the earliest securely dated specimen is unresolved. No competing formation or specific graphic corruption is documented in the cited accounts.
A modern dictionary also lists figurative stubbornness, star-name, zodiac, calendar, and surname uses. Their dates and connections to the animal sense are unresolved.

Supplied local data records Mandarin niú and Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese ngjuw and Old Chinese *[ŋ]ʷə. The character-specific Unihan record could not be accessed; these readings do not establish graphic formation, and 牛 is not analyzed as a phonetic component.

senses.text: The graph is interpreted as depicting the animal, and 牛 is reported in an inscription referring to cattle. The earliest securely dated occurrence is unresolved; this is the earliest supported sense, not a dated first use.

senses.period: Shuowen Jiezi; date of use not established here
senses.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry glosses 牛 as a large sacrificial animal. This dictionary gloss does not establish a separate earlier sense or the graph’s original meaning.

A modern dictionary lists this figurative sense, but its date and development from the animal sense are unresolved.

limitations.text: No dated corpus of written senses establishes the chronology or semantic connections among the animal, figurative, astronomical, calendar, zodiac, and surname uses.

overview.text: 牛 pictures an ox’s head and horns. It names the animal, meaning ox or cattle, and also serves as a character radical.
